reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: General
sections.body: Cost estimation for drilled shaft foundations is Step 15 in the overall design and construction process (Chapter 8). Preliminary estimates are used to compare drilled shafts with other technically feasible foundation systems. Final estimates made prior to bid for total project cost. Actual cost established through competitive bidding. Best approach to lowest overall cost: design competing foundation systems and request bids on each; additional engineering effort for alternatives is often offset by savings. No single formula provides highly accurate costs for a specific project prior to bidding. Contractors estimate based on time and materials. Historical bid data (state DOT bid tabs) and experience with constructability are the basis for good estimates.
key_points: Cost estimation is Step 15 in the overall design process (Chapter 8)
Preliminary: compare alternatives; Final: project cost estimate before bid
Design competing foundation alternatives — additional effort offset by savings from competitive bids
Historical bid data from state DOT websites is a valuable resource for cost estimates
sections.applicability: Cost estimation for drilled shaft foundations; alternative foundation comparison

sections.title: Factors Influencing Cost
sections.body: Key factors affecting drilled shaft costs: (1) Subsurface and site conditions — largest influence; rock hardness; trafficability; nearby structures; traffic control; underground utilities; overhead lines/bridges; cut-off elevation; low headroom (rigs cost ~3× open rig); (2) Shaft geometry — unit cost increases with depth; unit cost decreases with diameter increase up to ~8 ft for soil; larger diameter in hard rock more difficult and expensive; (3) Number of shafts — larger projects have lower unit costs as mobilization spread over more shafts; (4) Specifications and inspection procedures — 'method spec' (specific methods required) drives up cost; unreasonable NDT penalty provisions increase cost; (5) Obstructions — projects with no payment for any obstructions have large contingencies; paying for all obstructions reduces contingency; (6) Weather conditions — harsh winter affects productivity and cost; (7) Work time restrictions — night work and lane closures increase cost; (8) Location — travel and living costs; Alaska and Hawaii examples; (9) Schedule and penalty clauses; (10) Work rules — union/non-union; certified welder requirements; (11) Government regulations — environmental, safety, noise restrictions; (12) Equipment availability; (13) Concrete availability and price; (14) Contractor experience and ingenuity; (15) Material costs — steel price fluctuations; (16) Economic conditions and construction activity level; (17) Insurance, bonding, cost of money; (18) Contract terms and risk allocation; (19) General contractor fees and overhead. Survey findings (O'Neill and Reese 1999): rock socket construction ~3× overburden cost per unit length; wet alluvium with boulders ~2× soft socket cost; slurry or full-length casing ~1/3 more expensive than dry stable overburden.
key_points: Subsurface conditions: largest single cost influence
Low headroom rigs: ~3× cost of open rigs
Rock socket: ~3× per unit length cost compared to dry overburden
Slurry or full-length casing: ~1/3 more expensive than dry stable overburden
Method specifications: increase cost compared to performance specifications
Paying for all obstructions reduces contractor contingency vs. paying only for man-made
sections.applicability: Preliminary and final cost estimates; specification writing to reduce contingencies

sections.title: Commentary
sections.body: Many variables affect drilled shaft costs — no single formula provides highly accurate costs prior to bidding. Contractors estimate based on time and materials for specific conditions. Local cost information from historical awarded contracts is the best guide for preliminary comparisons. For final estimates, historical price data combined with constructability experience are essential. The prudent action is to select a contractor with necessary equipment, experienced personnel, and a record of high-quality construction regardless of whether foundation cost is small or large percentage of total project. Some agencies prequalify drilled shaft contractors to help assure quality.
key_points: No single formula provides accurate pre-bid cost estimates — too many site-specific variables
Historical bid tabs from state DOTs are the best reference for preliminary estimates
Contractor prequalification: some agencies require it to assure quality
Combining competing foundation alternatives in bid package often yields lowest overall cost

sections.title: Publicly Available Price Data
sections.body: State transportation agencies maintain databases of submitted bid prices ('bid tabs') accessible via websites. Historical price data provides snapshots of actual drilled shaft costs by state and region. Example: Texas DOT (TxDOT) bid tabs provide large sample because Texas uses many drilled shafts. Published price data should be adjusted for: inflation (use Engineering News-Record Construction Cost Index or similar); regional cost differences; project-specific difficulty factors. Published data may be in $/linear foot, $/cubic yard, or lump sum per shaft; must be converted to comparable basis for project estimates. FHWA and state DOTs also publish cost indices and guides.
key_points: State DOT bid tabs available on websites — valuable historical cost data
Adjust published data for: inflation (ENR Index), regional differences, project difficulty
Convert data to consistent basis ($/LF, $/CY, or lump sum) for fair comparison

sections.title: Contractor Cost Computation
sections.body: Contractor cost breakdown: variable costs + jobsite fixed costs + overhead + contingencies + markup = bid price. Variable costs: drilling (labor, equipment, tooling, consumables); casing (rental or purchase); slurry mixing, monitoring, disposal; concrete (materials, equipment, quality control, cylinders); reinforcing steel (materials, fabrication, handling); load testing (if required); NDT testing. Jobsite fixed costs: mobilization/demobilization; site utilities; supervision/management; small tools; safety equipment; survey. Overhead: company overhead applied as percentage of direct costs. Contingencies: subsurface risk; bid error; weather; schedule. Markup: profit margin; typically 5-15% depending on competition and market conditions. Unit prices established by dividing total cost estimate by number of units (LF of shaft, LY of concrete, etc.). Structural steel price and concrete pricing volatility can introduce significant uncertainty in estimates for future bid dates.
key_points: Bid price = variable costs + fixed costs + overhead + contingency + markup
Contingency reflects subsurface uncertainty — reduces when subsurface information is complete
Mobilization/demobilization: significant for small projects; negligible for large ones
Steel price and concrete price volatility add uncertainty for future bids

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter briefly addressed factors influencing drilled shaft costs and provided general guidance on estimating costs. Subsurface conditions are the single largest cost influence. No formula provides highly accurate pre-bid estimates. Use historical bid data from state DOTs adjusted for inflation and regional conditions as the basis for preliminary estimates. Design competing foundation alternatives and request competitive bids for the lowest overall cost. Contractor prequalification helps assure quality on drilled shaft projects.
